heroText: Khartoum is Sudan's capital at the dramatic meeting point of the Blue and White Nile, long home to the Khartoum National Museum, the historic Souq Omdurman and the whirling dervishes at Hamed al-Nil Tomb. Since 2023 the city has been affected by serious armed conflict, and Khartoum International Airport has been repeatedly closed, so travel here is not currently advisable. This guide covers Khartoum's landmarks and layout for reference and for future planning once conditions improve.

areas.name: Khartoum Centre
areas.text: Khartoum Centre is the historic downtown core along the Blue Nile, home to the National Museum, ministries and the Presidential Palace.

areas.name: Omdurman
areas.text: Omdurman is Khartoum's twin city across the Nile, known for its sprawling souq and the Friday whirling dervishes ceremony.

areas.name: Khartoum North (Bahri)
areas.text: Khartoum North, known as Bahri, is an industrial and residential district across the Blue Nile from the city centre.

areas.name: Tuti Island
areas.text: Tuti Island sits at the exact confluence of the Blue and White Nile, a small farming community reached by bridge or boat.

airports.name: Khartoum International Airport (KRT)
airports.text: Khartoum International Airport has been repeatedly closed and damaged amid the ongoing conflict since 2023, and travelers should check current status before making any plans.

airportTransfer.value: Compare road transfer time between Khartoum International Airport (KRT) and central Khartoum before choosing an airport-area or city-centre hotel.

stayOverview: Khartoum is not currently recommended for travel due to ongoing armed conflict, and this stay information is provided for reference. Historically Khartoum Centre offered the most convenient base near the National Museum and Presidential Palace, with Omdurman across the river known for its markets and Bahri as a quieter residential option.
hotelIntro: Hotel planning for Khartoum is currently on hold given the security situation; historically, Khartoum Centre held the main business hotels near government offices, while Omdurman and Bahri offered more local, lower-cost stays across the Nile.
rentalCars: Independent driving is not advisable under current conditions; historically a driver was recommended for crossing between Khartoum, Omdurman and Bahri across the Nile bridges.

travelTips.title: Airport status
travelTips.text: Verify whether Khartoum International Airport is operational before booking, since it has been repeatedly closed and damaged.

travelTips.title: Historical layout
travelTips.text: Note that Khartoum, Omdurman and Bahri sit across the Nile from one another, traditionally linked by several bridges.

travelTips.title: Cultural reference
travelTips.text: The Friday whirling dervishes ceremony at Hamed al-Nil Tomb in Omdurman was, prior to the conflict, one of Sudan's best-known cultural events.

history.text: Egypt shifted the seat of the colonial government from Wad Madani to Khartoum in 1823, which became a permanent settlement and underwent rapid development in the next decades.
A significant change took place in 1854, when most of the city was destroyed by heavy rains and floods.
Despite being fortified by trenches and a wall connecting the Blue and White Niles, the city was conquered by the Mahdists on 26 January 1885 and the entire garrison was annihilated.
Herbert Kitchener became Governor-General of the Sudan in September 1898, and began a programme of reconstruction, Khartoum was rebuilt according to a street plan in the shape of the Union Jack.
Under Reginald Wingate (1899–1916), the Governor-General's Palace in Khartoum was rebuilt using red bricks, with sandstone used for the corners.
The Gordon Memorial College (now the University of Khartoum) was opened in 1903, and a new railway to Port Sudan was completed in 1919.
Khartoum continued to grow after it was declared the capital of the newly independent Republic of Sudan in 1956.

On 3 June 2019, Khartoum was the site of the Khartoum massacre, where over 100 dissidents were murdered (the government said 61 were killed), hundreds more injured and 70 women raped by Rapid Support.
On 1 July 2020, activists demanded that al-Zibar Basha street in Khartoum be renamed.
